newsitem.title: GREENLAND: FEATURE - Greenland far away from possible self-sufficncy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Greenland far away from possible self-sufficncy.

text.p: The proud Inuit people of Greenland, given home rule under the Danish crown in 1979, would like to be independent economically, but their dreams of self-sufficiency will be hard to achieve.

Danish aid of three billion crowns ($524.6 million) annually provides 60 percent of the home rule government's revenue and is equal to 45 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) -- estimated at 6.7 billion crowns in 1994.
Income from fish exports provides the bulk of the remainder and it is a fickle industry where a relatively slight change in sea temperature can eradicate stocks.

Greenlanders have learnt that lesson only too well; they saw cod catches plummet from around 500,000 tonnes a year during the 1960s to a mere 1,404 tonnes in 1995 because of a two degree centigrade drop in average water temperatures.

"In Greenland we are especially vulnerable to shocks in the fishing industry. Ninety-five percent of our exports are fish products, 75 percent of which are prawns, the rest mainly Greenlandic halibut and cod," Prime Minister Lars Emil Johansen told journalists on a visit to the capital, Nuuk.
Greenland, though a part of the Kingdom of Denmark, withdrew from the European Union in 1982, putting it in the probably unique position of being a non-member region of an EU member-state.
It however sells a quota of 35,000 tonnes a year to the EU under a six-year deal bringing in 290 million crowns annually.
But fishing alone is a narrow base on which to build an econony and the country of 55,000 people wants desperately to build up tourism, mineral and petroleum industries.

Tourism is rising, from 3,300 visitors in 1987 to 15,000 in 1995, with 16,000 expected by the end of 1996. But officials say that with 1,200 tourist beds on the 2.1 million square km (810,900 square mile) island, capacity has now been reached.
Major expansion is planned and the government's goal is to double the 250 million crown tourism income estimated for 1996 to 500 million by 2002.
To achieve that aim it plans to increase hotel rooms, transport facilities and winter sports amenities.

It acknowledges that banks and finance houses have so far not been eager to put money into such projects and public financing will be necessary; the amount will be debated in the autumn session of the Greenland parliament.
One project gaining the interest of private enterprise is a proposed 500 million crown summer skiing centre at the Apussuit glacier, on the west coast, just south of the Arctic Circle.

U.S. company Greenland Outdoor has already signed an agreement contingent on the government putting the infrastructure in place but the final go ahead is likely to come in the year 2,000 at the earliest, Finance Minister Daniel Skifte said.
Greenland's greatest hope, and biggest gamble, is the prospect of a major discovery of oil or minerals.
Surveys indicate that the Fylla area, in ice-free waters 100 miles west of Nuuk could have oil and gas reserves to rival Norway's biggest North Sea field, Troll. But "could' is the key word.

"There is no riskier undertaking, it's a wildcat in the full sense of the word," said Erik Andersen of Greenland-based Canadian oil company Platinova A/S, which found hydrocarbons in test borings at Nuussuaq in the far north.
"You can never know, but we think there's a good chance," he said adding that 26 holes were drilled in Troll before oil was found while only five had so far been sunk in Fylla.

Two consortia had applied for exploration licences at Fylla, one group consisting of Denmark's DONG, Norway's Statoil and the U.S. company Phillips Petroleum and the other of French firms Total and Gulf Aquitaine.
Johansen said a decision could be made as early as September.
The Black Angel zinc mine, at Maarmorilik, on the west coast, closed in 1990 but Canadian firms prospecting for zinc in the north report promising results and there are signs of gold in the south.
As a spinoff from the search for nickel and copper, indications of kimberlite have been found, but so far no diamonds.

Greenland's natural beauty gives it serious potential as a tourist destination if the high cost of travel and accommodation can be brought down. Its geology also indicates a strong probability of mineral wealth.
But it will take time to build up a tourist infrastructure, time to find minerals and possibly wait until market conditions make their extraction viable.
Even if oil were found tomorrow it would take five-10 years before production could begin. With gas the time needed to build the necessary facilities is nearer 20 years.
Greenland may well be able to pay its own way in future, but all the indications are that it may be the next generation which enjoys the benefits. ($1=5.718 Danish Crown)
